title: jenkinsir.com
summary: A bilingual Medicare and ACA education website I built and run as a licensed agent: about 1,900 pages in English and Spanish, an assistant that can't invent advice, and automated checks before every release.
role: Owner and builder. I set the requirements, made the architecture and compliance decisions, checked the accuracy of every figure, and verified each release. Built with AI coding tools (Lovable to start, then Claude Code).
why: People turning 65 get buried in mailers and TV ads. As a licensed agent in Utah and Wyoming, I wanted one place where families could get straight, sourced answers in English or Spanish before talking to anyone.
learned: More isn't better. Publishing hundreds of short articles at once got the site demoted in Google's August 2026 spam update. I took 378 thin posts out of Google's index and now publish fewer, longer ones on a steady schedule.
In a regulated field, predictable beats clever. The assistant only gives pre-written, reviewed answers, so it can't invent a plan recommendation.
Tests are how I trust AI-written code. Bugs that reached production, like a popup that crashed on open, became automated checks. Nine now run before each release.
approach: TanStack Start (React and TypeScript), server-rendered on Vercel. Route files stay tiny and each page loads only the data it needs, so a large content library stays fast. Forms post to the site's own API, which filters spam without ever blocking a real person and files each lead in a Google Sheet. Pages for Nevada and Idaho route visitors to the agents licensed there.
demonstrates: Running a real production system: performance at scale, SEO in two languages, accessibility for an older audience, analytics that never collect personal details, and compliance rules built into the design.
limit: The code is private because the site is tied to my insurance work. It was built with AI coding tools, so my part is the product and compliance decisions, the accuracy of the content, and verifying each release.

title: Client Inquiry Pipeline
summary: A serverless AWS pipeline that saves quote requests as structured records, so questions like "which products do people ask about most?" are answered with SQL instead of by digging through an inbox.
role: Designed and built it end to end: the architecture, the AWS setup (first by hand, then as code), the Lambda function, the SQL, the tests and the CI. Claude helped as a coding assistant.
why: I wanted to learn AWS on a problem I know from insurance. A quote form that only sends an email can't answer simple questions, like which products people ask about most or how many inquiries came in this week.
learned: Build it twice. Recreating the hand-built backend as code exposed a crash on malformed input. The fixed version returns a clean error.
CORS is a browser rule, not security. Real protection comes from least-privilege access: the function can write new records but can never read or delete them.
Store times in UTC and report in local time, or a day's numbers land on the wrong date.
approach: A static form on S3 and CloudFront posts to an API Gateway endpoint. A Python Lambda function validates each inquiry and saves it as a JSON file in a private S3 bucket, and Athena runs SQL over those files. The backend is also defined as code with AWS SAM, and 12 unit tests plus a template check run on every push through GitHub Actions.
demonstrates: Designing a small data pipeline around a business question, applying least-privilege access and server-side validation, and finding a bug by building the backend twice.
limit: A learning project on fake data only. The analytics come from 101 generated inquiries and are not market findings. The API has no authentication; it is throttled to 5 requests a second.
skills: AWS (S3, Lambda, API Gateway, Athena, CloudFront)

title: Text From Sheet
status: Public · not yet field-tested on a phone
summary: Texts a spreadsheet of contacts from a person's own phone number: personalized, paced, and built with guardrails against mistakes.
role: Gathered the requirements from the person who needed it, defined the safety rules, and verified the result with 153 automated tests. Claude helped as a coding assistant.
why: A non-technical family member needed to text a few hundred people who know him, from his own number. Bulk-texting services need accounts, fees and carrier registration, and sending by hand is slow and error-prone.
learned: Keep the rules in tested code and the screens thin. One rules engine powers both the web page and the Android sender.

Respect the platform's limits. A web page can't send texts by itself, so the simple version keeps a person in the loop, and the automatic sender is a separate, rate-limited tool that needs typed approval.
Privacy by design: there is no server, so the contact list never leaves the phone.
approach: A Python rules engine normalizes phone numbers and enforces consent, opt-out and do-not-text lists, duplicate removal, and sensitive-data blocking. An Android (Termux) sender paces texts about one a minute between 8am and 6pm after one typed approval, logs every send so it can resume, and runs from one-tap home-screen buttons. A no-install web app offers a review-each-text version.
demonstrates: Turning a real person's request into requirements, building controls against misuse and compliance mistakes, and proving the logic with automated tests.
limit: Tests use simulated senders; it hasn't been field-tested on a phone yet. Delivery isn't confirmed, picture texts need one tap per person (an Android limit), and all sample data is fictional.

title: AI For Life
summary: The website for the AI For Life student club: beginner tool walkthroughs with business use cases, a searchable glossary, a prompt library, and a way for members to contribute and get credit.
role: Founded the club's website and its contribution process, wrote the first tool guides, glossary and roadmap, and review and merge members' pull requests.
why: Our club needed one place where beginners could start, and members needed a way to get visible, verifiable credit for what they contribute.
learned: Design for people who've never used Git. Edits happen in the browser and arrive as pull requests I review.
Automate the fragile parts. One script rebuilds the search index and sitemap and checks every link, so a beginner's edit can't break the site.
Write instructions for AI helpers too. A CLAUDE.md file keeps members' AI assistants following the site's rules.
approach: Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript published by GitHub Pages, with no build step so anyone can edit it. Site-wide search, an installable web app with offline support, and a contributors page that turns merged pull requests into résumé proof.
demonstrates: Explaining technical topics to beginners, running an open contribution workflow, and keeping a community site easy to maintain.
limit: An educational resource. AI tools change fast, so the guides need ongoing review.
